region: Hualien, the East Rift Valley, Taitung, Pingtung, Tainan and Alishan
title: Taiwan — Between Mountains and the Pacific
subtitle: Down the east coast by car, up into the Alishan cloud forest, ending in the temples and forts of Tainan
summary: A 13-day focused route: marble gorges and Pacific cliffs around Hualien, rice valleys and hot springs in the East Rift Valley, Amis, Bunun and Paiwan communities, Tainan's 17th-century forts, and sunrise above Alishan's tea slopes.
introduction: You land at Taoyuan, take the Taroko Express to Hualien and collect a seven-seater the next morning. Highway 8 into Taroko Gorge opens only in fixed time windows, so the day is built around them. Then you drive south along the East Rift Valley: iron-rich hot springs at Ruisui, Amis villages near Guangfu, rice paddies at Chishang, two nights in tents beside the Pacific. Paiwan carving in Sandimen leads to Tainan, where Dutch and Qing forts stand beside street-food alleys. A mountain railway and a bus climb to Alishan for sunrise above the tea slopes before the high-speed train back to Taipei.

exceptional.vsOman: Oman is arid, empty and tent-based; Taiwan is humid, dense and green, with convenience stores and hot springs every 30 km. The challenge is not self-sufficiency in a desert but reading rapidly changing mountain weather and road-opening windows, and getting inside living indigenous and Han Chinese traditions rather than passing through empty landscapes.
exceptional.vsPackageTourism: Standard Taiwan tours run a coach circuit of Taipei, Sun Moon Lake, Alishan and Taroko in 6–8 days. This route goes slowly down the less-visited east coast by car, camps on the Pacific side, spends a night in a Paiwan town and a night at 2,200 m, and leaves two full days in Tainan.
exceptional.vsPortfolio: No other destination in the portfolio combines 3,000 m-class mountain scenery, a typhoon-and-earthquake-shaped Pacific coastline, five-plus indigenous peoples with active cultural programmes, a dense Taoist and Buddhist temple tradition, a 17th-century Dutch fort, and a hot-spring culture — all with a rail and HSR safety net, drinkable-quality food hygiene and no security warnings.

duration.note: Day 1 outbound departure, Day 13 arrival in Paris (overnight return flight leaves Day 12 evening).

recommendedTravelWindow.rationale: Starting after Lunar New Year (6 Feb) and the 27 Feb–1 Mar Peace Memorial Day weekend avoids the busiest travel periods; March is a little warmer and drier on the east coast than February, though Alishan is still cool. Late March gives the first Alishan cherry blossoms. The window also falls in Ramadan, which is not relevant in Taiwan.

februarySuitability.summary: Cool, grey northeast-monsoon weather on the Hualien coast and in the north, snow possible at Hehuanshan, and Lunar New Year (6 Feb) pushes up prices and fills trains and rentals. Taitung and Tainan are drier and sunnier. A mid- to late-February trip is workable but weather-dependent.

marchSuitability.summary: Warmer (day 20–25 °C on the lowlands), fewer holiday crowds, longer days, and Alishan cherry-blossom season starting. Still unsettled in the north and Hualien area, with frequent drizzle; mountain roads are clear of snow in most years.

climate.regionNote: Approximate ranges for Hualien, Taitung and Tainan lowlands, compiled from commercial climate summaries (weather2travel, weather-and-climate) and not official CWA normals; sources disagree on Hualien rainfall (about 140–290 mm in March). Alishan (2,200 m) is typically 8–10 °C cooler and wetter: roughly 8–14 °C by day, 3–7 °C at night in February.

february.rainfall: Frequent light rain in Hualien and the north (about 15–18 rain days); Taitung and Tainan drier
february.notes: Northeast monsoon brings cloud and drizzle to the north and the Hualien coast. Highway 8 and 14A can close for rock fall or ice. Alishan is cold and often misty.

march.rainfall: Frequent showers on the east coast, heaviest in the north; plum rains begin in late spring
march.notes: Warmer and slightly more settled in the south. Layers needed in the mountains. Spring fog at Alishan.

climate.snowAndMountainAccess: Snow occurs on Hehuanshan (Highway 14A) in some Februaries and the highway is closed overnight or chains required. Yushan and Xueshan (3,500 m+) are in snow-season rules: snow-climbing certification and equipment required, so high-mountain routes are not in this plan. Alishan (2,200 m) is normally frost-free.
climate.seaConditions: Pacific swell and the northeast monsoon make swimming unsafe on most east-coast beaches in winter; coastal sections of Highway 11 can be closed in high waves.
climate.airQuality: Good on the east coast; Taipei and the western plain are moderate, with winter-spring haze episodes.
climate.wildlifeSeasonality: Not a wildlife-led trip: occasional dolphin sightings off Hualien are possible; early cherry blossom at Alishan from mid-March.

holidaysAndFestivals.name: Lunar New Year
holidaysAndFestivals.impact: Peak domestic travel: HSR and TRA sell out within hours of booking opening, rental cars and rural guesthouses are expensive, many family-run restaurants close for several days. Avoided in the recommended March window.

holidaysAndFestivals.name: Lantern Festival
holidaysAndFestivals.dates: ≈ 20–21 Feb 2027 (15th day of the first lunar month)
holidaysAndFestivals.impact: Local festivities including lanterns in Tainan and Pingxi; crowds in some towns. Not in March window.

holidaysAndFestivals.name: Peace Memorial Day (228)
holidaysAndFestivals.impact: Busy weekend for domestic travel; avoided in March window.

climate.ramadan2027: Not relevant: Taiwan has no Ramadan-related closures; halal food is limited outside Muslim-friendly restaurants in Taipei and Hualien.
climate.lunarNewYear2027: Lunar New Year's Day is Saturday 6 February 2027 with the government break running 4–10 February. Inside Feb the whole country moves, prices spike, and shops close for several days. A March departure avoids it entirely. If travelling in February, avoid the period 4–14 February.
climate.tourismDemand: Low to moderate in March outside holiday weekends; Taroko and Alishan are busy at weekends. Taroko receives far fewer visitors than before April 2024 because of closures.
climate.flightPriceSeasonality: Fares peak around Lunar New Year and in July–August; mid-January to mid-March non-holiday dates are relatively cheaper. EVA Air listed round trips from about EUR 811 to EUR 924 for Feb–Mar 2027 on the day checked.

geography.summary: A 3,000 m mountain spine drops to the Pacific on the east and to the western plain; the narrow East Rift Valley separates the Central Range from the Coastal Range.
geography.distinctive: Taiwan has more than 200 peaks above 3,000 m on an island the size of the Netherlands, a plate-collision zone that creates the East Rift Valley and marble gorges such as Taroko, and a hot-spring culture dating from the Japanese era.

landscapes.name: Taroko Gorge
landscapes.description: Marble gorge cut by the Liwu River; trails remain closed after the April 2024 earthquake but the road section is visitable in set windows.

landscapes.name: East Rift Valley (Ruisui–Chishang)
landscapes.description: Rice paddies and farmland between the Central and Coastal Ranges, with hot springs at Ruisui.

landscapes.name: Qingshui Cliff and Highway 11 coast
landscapes.description: Sea cliffs rising to 800 m and a quiet Pacific coast road with fishing ports and Amis villages.

landscapes.name: Alishan cloud forest
landscapes.description: Giant cypress groves, tea terraces and a narrow-gauge forest railway at 2,200 m.

culture.summary: Austronesian indigenous peoples (Amis, Truku, Bunun, Paiwan, Rukai), Hokkien and Hakka Han settlement, Dutch, Spanish, Qing and Japanese layers, and a living Taoist and Buddhist temple culture.

culturalHighlights.name: Tainan old city
culturalHighlights.description: Taiwan's first capital: Fort Zeelandia (Anping), Chihkan Tower (Fort Provintia), the Confucius Temple of 1665, Grand Matsu Temple, and some 1,600 temples in the city region.

culturalHighlights.name: Amis community at Fata'an, Guangfu
culturalHighlights.description: Amis village with a folklore centre and community-run programmes on fish-trap, food and ceremony. Choose community-run options rather than staged shows.

culturalHighlights.name: Sandimen and the Paiwan / Rukai villages
culturalHighlights.description: Paiwan wood carving, glass beads and Rukai stone-slab houses; visit local workshops and the nearby Indigenous Peoples Cultural Park.

culturalHighlights.name: Truku culture around Taroko
culturalHighlights.description: The Truku are Taroko's original inhabitants; community-run visits and tours near Tianxiang and Buluowan are available through local operators.

culturalHighlights.name: Temples and night markets
culturalHighlights.description: Longshan Temple in Taipei, Tainan's Matsu temples, and night markets such as Dongdamen in Hualien and Garden/Flower in Tainan.

adventureHighlights.name: Taroko Gorge by self-drive and short walks
adventureHighlights.description: Highway 8 through Taroko is open to self-drive vehicles only in set time windows (about 06:30–08:00, 10:00, 12:00–13:00, 15:00, 17:00–17:30 according to a March–August 2026 report; confirm). The popular Shakadang, Zhuilu and Swallow Grotto trails remain closed; Tianxiang and its short trails are open.

adventureHighlights.name: Hot-spring soaking in the East Rift Valley and Beitou
adventureHighlights.description: Ruisui's hot springs and Beitou's Japanese-era bathing district; no technical skills.

adventureHighlights.name: Cycling Chishang paddies and Pacific coast camping
adventureHighlights.description: Flat cycling routes in Chishang and two nights at licensed campsites near the Pacific; roads in the Coastal Range can be closed after rain or earthquakes.

adventureHighlights.name: Alishan sunrise and forest railway
adventureHighlights.description: Pre-dawn train or bus to Zhushan viewpoint at 2,400 m; cold (about 3–7 °C) and frequent cloud; the railway is closed during typhoons and for maintenance.

signatureExperiences.title: Highway 8 into Taroko Gorge in the time windows
signatureExperiences.description: Enter the gorge in an early window, walk the open Tianxiang and Xiangde Temple trails, and see the marble walls from viewpoints and bridges before the next window opens.
signatureExperiences.whyDistinctive: Taroko in 2026–27 is a recovering park: far fewer visitors, closed trails, and a road that opens only at set times. Seeing it now is different from the packed pre-2024 experience, and requires patience.
signatureExperiences.howToOrganise: Rent the car in Hualien on Day 3, check the Taroko National Park traffic page and Highway Bureau notices the night before, enter the gorge in the first window, and return in the 12:00–13:00 window. Join a locally run Truku community tour if offered at the visitor centre.
signatureExperiences.costNote: Park entry is free; cost shown is a share of a half-day community guide for the group.

signatureExperiences.title: Two nights camping by the Pacific and the East Rift Valley
signatureExperiences.description: Cycle the Chishang rice fields, pitch tents at licensed campsites in the valley and on the Highway 11 coast, and cook from local markets.
signatureExperiences.whyDistinctive: It keeps the group's camping tradition in a country with few legal wild-camping options; the campsites are working farms or licensed sites with rental tents and mats.
signatureExperiences.howToOrganise: Book licensed campsites in advance (only a small share of Taiwan's campsites are fully licensed). Rent tents and mats from the site. Night temperatures in March are about 13–16 °C.
signatureExperiences.costNote: Two tents × two nights including gear rental, split by four.

signatureExperiences.title: A night in Sandimen with Paiwan and Rukai craft traditions
signatureExperiences.description: Stay in a locally run guesthouse, visit carving and glass-bead workshops, and talk to craftspeople who sell directly.
signatureExperiences.whyDistinctive: A direct, paid exchange with indigenous makers rather than a staged performance.
signatureExperiences.howToOrganise: Book a locally run homestay or guesthouse; arrange a workshop session with the Sandimen township cultural centre or the Indigenous Peoples Cultural Park. Ask hosts what is appropriate to photograph.
signatureExperiences.costNote: Workshop or entry fee; accommodation is in the accommodation budget lines.

signatureExperiences.title: Tainan across four centuries
signatureExperiences.description: Walk from Fort Zeelandia to Chihkan Tower, the Confucius Temple, Shennong Street and Matsu temples, eating at breakfast stalls and night markets.
signatureExperiences.whyDistinctive: Taiwan's oldest city layers Dutch, Ming-loyalist, Qing and Japanese history in a walkable centre with exceptional local food.
signatureExperiences.howToOrganise: Two nights in a guesthouse near the old centre; walk and use buses or bicycles; plan a food route for breakfast soups, beef soup and dan-zai noodles.
signatureExperiences.costNote: Entry fees to forts and museums.

signatureExperiences.title: Alishan sunrise and the forest railway
signatureExperiences.description: Overnight at 2,200 m, take the pre-dawn train to the viewpoint, walk through cypress groves and visit tea farms.
signatureExperiences.whyDistinctive: A narrow-gauge mountain railway among giant cypress, with sunrise above a sea of cloud on clear mornings.
signatureExperiences.location: Alishan National Scenic Area, Chiayi County
signatureExperiences.howToOrganise: Reserve the railway and a guesthouse before the trip; take the bus from Chiayi; check the Forest and Nature Conservation Agency notices for closures.
signatureExperiences.costNote: Railway fare, scenic-area entry and bus share.

travelStyle.summary: Rail and a rented 7-seater on the east coast, bus, TRA and high-speed rail elsewhere; short walks and cycling rather than long treks.

transport.summary: Taiwan has dense rail, HSR, bus and rental-car options. Rail (Taroko Express, Puyuma) reaches Hualien and Taitung; Highway 9 and Highway 11 on the east coast and Highway 8 through Taroko are best done by car.

modes.description: Taipei to Hualien in about 2 hours; reserve in advance outside holiday periods.
Hualien (Day 3) to Tainan (Day 8) with a one-way fee; two drivers share driving.
Chiayi to Taipei in about 1.5 hours on Day 11; Tainan to Chiayi in about 11 minutes.
Chiayi to Alishan by bus (about 2.5 hours) or railway when running; check closures after storms.
Airport MRT to Taipei Main Station; MRT to Beitou.

transport.carRental: Rental from Hualien station or airport, with one-way drop at Tainan HSR station (one-way fee varies by vehicle and date; shown only during booking). Major networks include Hotai (National/Enterprise partner), iRent and local firms; credit card in the driver's name is required; additional-driver fee about NT$180 per day at Hotai's Tainan HSR branch, and the second driver must be present at pick-up. Prices not verified: planning estimate EUR 110 per day for a 7-seater.

drivingRequirements.summary: Self-drive is routine for foreign visitors in Taiwan. Taiwan drives on the right. Mountain roads need care, scooter traffic is dense, and Highway 8 in Taroko has time-window access and rockfall.
drivingRequirements.internationalDrivingPermit: Rental firms generally require a valid home licence plus an International Driving Permit under the 1949 Geneva or 1968 Vienna Convention; non-governmental IDPs are not accepted. Acceptance depends on the licence country: Taiwan's Directorate General of Highways publishes a reciprocal-country table (not verified for any specific country here). IDPs from some countries (for example Estonia, China, South Korea, Brazil, Vietnam, UAE, Thailand) have been reported as not accepted. Check the licence country against the DGH table and the rental firm's terms before booking.
drivingRequirements.licenceNotes: Two of the four hold car licences and would be the named drivers; both must present passport, home licence, IDP if required, and a credit card at pick-up. The two non-drivers do not drive. Taiwan's rules on how long a foreign licence or IDP is valid for visitors differ between sources; confirm before booking.
drivingRequirements.motorcycleNotes: Nobody rides a scooter or motorcycle without the legally required licence: a motorcycle endorsement on the home licence and an IDP covering motorcycles are typically required, and unlicensed rentals are a legal and insurance risk. Alternatives: ride as a passenger with a licensed driver, use the car, taxis, buses, bicycles (Chishang), electric bicycles, TRA and MRT.
drivingRequirements.recommendedApproach: Car only for Days 3–8 on the east coast and the road to Sandimen; use trains and buses elsewhere. Two licensed drivers share driving with a limit of about 3–4 hours at a time.

accommodation.summary: Guesthouses and B&Bs in Hualien, Ruisui, Sandimen, Tainan and Alishan; licensed farm and coastal campsites for two nights; a hotel near Beitou or Taipei Main Station for the final night.

camping.summary: Camping is allowed only at designated campsites; wild camping outside them can be fined in national parks (examples reported at NT$1,500–3,000), and many commercial campsites are unlicensed. Rental tents and mats are available, but two nights is realistic, not a camping expedition.

physicalDifficulty.label: moderate
physicalDifficulty.summary: Short walks and cycling, long days of driving and stairs at temples; the altitude at Alishan (2,200 m) is mild. Cold and wet at Alishan in March.

itinerary.summary: 13 days: Taipei, Hualien and Taroko, the East Rift Valley, a two-night camping stretch near the Pacific, Sandimen, two days in Tainan, Alishan, and Taipei. Rental car from Day 3 to Day 8.

security.summary: No UK warnings, Dutch advice green and no restrictions found for the east-coast and Tainan route. France Diplomatie places the whole territory in normal vigilance and the US rates Taiwan Level 1 (both read by A21 on 27 Nov 2026). Ordinary risks are earthquakes, mountain road closures and heavy rain.
security.assessedRoute: Taipei, Hualien County (Taroko), East Rift Valley, Taitung County, Pingtung County (Sandimen), Tainan, Chiayi County (Alishan), Taipei

advisories.level: Vigilance normale (green) for the whole territory (zone text updated 13 Mar 2026; security page read 27 Nov 2026)
No 'against travel' warnings on the page; updated 18 Nov 2026 with drug-offence information

advisories.routeImpact: None; typhoons May-November, earthquakes and landslides noted. Updated 20 Oct 2026.

conflictRisk.note: No active conflict on the route; cross-strait tension and military exercises are a background risk that can disrupt flights or airspace at short notice but is not treated by the advisories reviewed as an obstacle to travel.

terrorismRisk.note: No material terrorism risk identified in the advisories reviewed.

regionalRestrictions: Taroko National Park trails and Highway 8 have restricted access after the April 2024 earthquake and later typhoons; follow park closures.
Highway 9 had a reported lane closure near Duoliang (km 401) in October 2026 after Typhoon Champi.
Drug laws are very strict: possession and use of any illegal drug, including cannabis, is a serious offence.
ordinaryRisks: Earthquakes (the Hualien area is seismically active; April 2024 magnitude 7.4 event) and landslides.
Rockfall on mountain roads and closures after rain.
Dense scooter traffic and road accidents.
Typhoons are June to November and not expected in the window, but late-season storms in autumn have closed roads and rail.
Cold and wet weather at Alishan.
security.medicalAccess: Good: modern hospitals in Hualien, Taitung, Tainan, Chiayi and Taipei; National Health Insurance does not cover visitors, so insurance is needed.
security.insuranceConsiderations: Take travel insurance with medical and repatriation cover; confirm that it covers earthquake-related disruption and car rental excess and does not exclude cross-strait military-conflict events you may want covered.
security.reassessmentRequired: Re-check all advisories before booking and two weeks before departure; triggers include a change in cross-strait military activity, a major earthquake or typhoon affecting Hualien or Taitung, and Taroko or Highway 9 closure notices.

practicalRequirements.visa: Depends on nationality; many Western nationalities enter visa-free for up to 90 days (for example French citizens, per the Taipei Representative Office in France). Check each traveller's passport; this file does not assume passports.
practicalRequirements.entry: Onward or return ticket is required; the online arrival card may be required; check immigration and BOCA pages for the passport held.
practicalRequirements.passportValidity: At least 6 months beyond arrival is stated for French passports; check for other nationalities.
permits: No mountain permits are used in this plan; high-mountain routes (Yushan, Xueshan) need park and police permits and in snow season certified snow skills, so they are excluded.
practicalRequirements.insurance: Travel insurance with medical, repatriation and trekking cover.
practicalRequirements.connectivity: Good: 4G and 5G, eSIM and airport SIM cards; weaker in mountain valleys.
practicalRequirements.payments: Cards widely accepted in cities; cash needed at markets, campsites and rural guesthouses. EasyCard or iPASS for transport.
practicalRequirements.medical: Bring routine medicines; pharmacies are widespread; tap water is generally boiled before drinking.
practicalRequirements.fuel: Petrol stations are frequent; 95 octane is standard for rental cars.
equipment: Sleeping bag liners for rented tents

advantages: Compact, safe, well-organised country with rail and HSR backup for every leg.
Four distinct landscapes and several living indigenous cultures within one short route.
Excellent food hygiene and street food.
Hot springs and temples at every level of budget.
disadvantages: Taroko's main trails remain closed; the park is a damaged version of its former self.
East-coast weather in February and March is damp and grey.
Camping is limited to licensed sites; wild camping is not realistic.
Realistic total is in the exceptional budget band because flights and a rental car with one-way drop are costly.

Whether Taiwan accepts the travellers' driving licence and IDP type, and for how long.
Highway 9 south link and Highway 11 coastal road conditions after the 2026 typhoon season.
